implementation_notes: Scala/JVM inherits the Java tooling (async-profiler, JMH, JFR) and its wins, and adds Scala-specific ones: a case class in a hot loop allocates unless it is a primitive-specialised collection, a Vector or a List has its own indirection (an Array[Double] streams where a List[Double] boxes each element), and the standard collections (List, Map) have per-operation cost that a while loop over an Array does not. The most common measured Scala hotspot is boxing and collection overhead rather than arithmetic, exactly as in Java. JMH with warm-up is the benchmark (JIT tiering), and Scala.js and Scala Native have entirely different performance characteristics - Scala.js has no JIT (so no inlining), and Scala Native uses LLVM - so an optimisation tuned on the JVM does not transfer.
idiom_name: async-profiler / JFR attribution plus JMH with warm-up; boxing and collection overhead are the usual Scala/JVM wins
pitfalls: Boxing: List[Double] or Vector[Double] box every element; Array[Double] is a primitive array and streams - the most common measured Scala hotspot.
Collection-API overhead in a hot loop (List/Vector per-element cost) where an indexed loop over an Array is much faster.
A case class in a hot loop allocates unless the collection is primitive-specialised.
Benchmarking without @Warmup measures the interpreted tier.
Scala.js (no JIT) and Scala Native (LLVM) behave differently from the JVM; an optimisation tuned on the JVM does not transfer.
